easy.explanation: The Lord says, “I will be the God of all the families of Israel.”
easy.q: What does the Lord promise to be to Israel?

easy.explanation: The virgin of Israel will be adorned with tabrets and go forth in dances.
easy.q: What will Israel do after being rebuilt?

answers: On the islands of the sea
easy.explanation: The Lord says, “Thou shalt yet plant vines upon the mountains of Samaria.”
easy.q: Where will Israel plant vineyards?

medium.explanation: The Lord says, “I have loved thee with an everlasting love: therefore with lovingkindness have I drawn thee.”
medium.q: What does everlasting love lead the Lord to do?

answers: Return to Zion and to the Lord
medium.explanation: The watchmen call the people to go up to Zion unto the Lord their God.
medium.q: What does the cry, “Arise ye, and let us go up to Zion,” express?

medium.explanation: The context of dancing shows that a tabret is a musical drum.
medium.q: What is a “tabret” in this passage?

answers: Israel changes from a remnant to a restored and joyful people
challenge.explanation: The passage moves from those left by the sword to rebuilding, planting, dancing, and returning.
challenge.q: What major change is described in these verses?

answers: They show renewed settlement and stability
They show that Israel must flee the land
challenge.explanation: Planting and eating from vineyards portrays settled life restored in the land.
challenge.q: How do the vineyards contribute to the picture of restoration?

answers: The return is communal and national
The return concerns only one person
challenge.explanation: The calls to sing, praise, and go to Zion describe a shared national return.
challenge.q: What can be inferred from the public calls to sing, praise, and go to Zion?

paragraphs.title: Gathering the Exiles and Redemptive Abundance

answers: From the north country and the coasts of the earth
easy.explanation: The Lord will bring them from the north country and gather them from the coasts of the earth.
easy.q: From where will the Lord gather Israel?

answers: The blind, the lame, and pregnant women
easy.explanation: The passage specifically includes the blind, the lame, the woman with child, and her that travaileth.
easy.q: Who is included among those returning?

answers: By rivers of waters in a straight way
Through a dry wilderness without water
easy.explanation: He will cause them to walk by rivers of waters in a straight way where they will not stumble.
easy.q: How will the Lord lead the returning people?

answers: To show that the vulnerable are included
To show that they must remain in exile
To show that only they will rule
medium.explanation: Their inclusion emphasizes that the gathering is wide and compassionate.
medium.q: Why are the blind, lame, and pregnant women mentioned?

answers: It explains His care and protection
It means they will remain children forever
medium.explanation: The Lord says, “I am a father to Israel,” and therefore leads them safely.
medium.q: How does the Lord’s fatherly relationship to Israel relate to His leading them?

answers: The distant edges or farthest regions of the earth
medium.explanation: The phrase refers to faraway regions from which the exiles will be gathered.
medium.q: What does “the coasts of the earth” mean here?

challenge.explanation: The Lord will gather and keep Israel “as a shepherd doth his flock.”
challenge.q: What image describes how the Lord will keep the returning people?

challenge.explanation: A watered garden pictures fullness, refreshment, and restored well-being.
challenge.q: What does the phrase “their soul shall be as a watered garden” express?

challenge.explanation: The Lord promises to turn mourning into joy and make the people rejoice from their sorrow.
challenge.q: How is joy connected with consolation in this passage?

easy.explanation: The passage says, “Rahel weeping for her children.”
easy.q: For whom is Rachel weeping?

easy.explanation: The Lord says, “Refrain thy voice from weeping, and thine eyes from tears.”
easy.q: What does the Lord tell Rachel to refrain from?

easy.explanation: The Lord promises that their work will be rewarded and that they will return to their own border.
easy.q: What is promised to Rachel’s children?

answers: It represents the grief of the people
It explains the building of Jerusalem
medium.explanation: Rachel’s mourning symbolizes the national grief over children who are absent.
medium.q: How does Rachel’s weeping relate to Israel’s sorrow?

answers: Chastening, repentance, shame, and a plea to return
medium.explanation: Ephraim acknowledges chastening, repents, feels shame, and says, “Turn thou me.”
medium.q: What sequence is described in Ephraim’s confession?

answers: A lack of discipline or submission
medium.explanation: The image describes Ephraim as needing correction and becoming accustomed to the proper way.
medium.q: What does “a bullock unaccustomed to the yoke” suggest?

answers: The passage moves from absence and grief to hope and return
It moves from hope to threat
It moves from joy to destruction
challenge.explanation: Rachel weeps because her children are gone, but the Lord promises their return and future hope.
challenge.q: What is the main change between Rachel’s words and the Lord’s answer?

answers: It includes recognition, shame, and a desire to return
It depends only on material wealth
challenge.explanation: Ephraim admits his fault, is ashamed, and asks to be turned back.
challenge.q: What does Ephraim’s repentance teach about returning to God?

answers: Ephraim is described as a dear and pleasant child
challenge.explanation: The Lord says, “Is Ephraim my dear son?” and promises, “I will surely have mercy upon him.”
challenge.q: Why does the Lord respond to Ephraim with mercy?

paragraphs.title: The Daughter Returning to Her Path

easy.explanation: The Lord says, “Set thee up waymarks, make thee high heaps.”
easy.q: What is Israel told to set up?

easy.explanation: The Lord says, “Turn again, O virgin of Israel, turn again to these thy cities.”
easy.q: Where is Israel told to return?

easy.explanation: The Lord says, “I have replenished every sorrowful soul.”
easy.q: What will the Lord replenish?

answers: To mark the way of return
medium.explanation: They help identify the highway and the way that Israel previously traveled.
medium.q: Why are waymarks and high heaps needed?

answers: It allows the land to be settled again
It leads Judah to abandon the land
medium.explanation: The following verses describe Judah being inhabited by husbandmen and shepherds.
medium.q: How does returning to the cities relate to the blessing of the land?

answers: A daughter who has turned away and is called to return
medium.explanation: The phrase describes Israel’s turning away and the Lord’s call to turn again.
medium.q: What does “backsliding daughter” mean in context?

answers: Israel has strayed but is invited to return
Israel has no relationship with the Lord
challenge.explanation: The Lord describes Israel as backsliding but calls her to return to her cities.
challenge.q: What does the image of the “backsliding daughter” communicate?

answers: Geographical return is accompanied by inner renewal
The road exists only for commerce
The cities remain desolate and hopeless
challenge.explanation: The return to inhabited cities is joined with the Lord’s replenishing of weary and sorrowful souls.
challenge.q: How are the road, the cities, and the sorrowful souls connected?

answers: An extraordinary act of renewal is taking place
The Lord has no part in the change
challenge.explanation: The statement emphasizes a remarkable new work connected with restoration.
challenge.q: What does “the Lord hath created a new thing in the earth” suggest?

answers: The house of Israel and the house of Judah
Only the cities of the nations
easy.explanation: The Lord will sow “the house of Israel and the house of Judah.”
easy.q: What will the Lord sow again?

easy.explanation: He says, “So will I watch over them, to build, and to plant.”
easy.q: What will the Lord do after plucking up and destroying?

answers: Everyone will die for his own iniquity
Children will always bear their fathers’ sins
easy.explanation: The passage says, “Every one shall die for his own iniquity.”
easy.q: What will be the principle of responsibility?

answers: He previously destroyed, but will later build and plant
He previously built, but will later destroy
He previously gathered, but will only scatter
medium.explanation: The passage contrasts plucking up, breaking down, and destroying with building and planting.
medium.q: What contrast appears between the Lord’s past and future actions?

answers: After awakening, his sleep was sweet
medium.explanation: The prophet says, “Upon this I awaked, and beheld; and my sleep was sweet unto me.”
medium.q: How is the prophet’s rest connected with the vision?

answers: Children suffer because of their fathers’ actions
medium.explanation: The saying describes children experiencing consequences for what their fathers did.
medium.q: What does the saying about sour grapes mean?

answers: Guilt always passes from father to son
challenge.explanation: The next verse states that every person will die for his or her own iniquity.
challenge.q: What moral change is presented in the teaching about sour grapes?

answers: They portray both renewed people and restored life
They express giving up the land
challenge.explanation: Sowing pictures the renewal of the people, while building and planting picture the restoration of their life.
challenge.q: How do the images of sowing and building complement each other?

answers: The same Lord who judged will also restore
The Lord becomes a different deity
The past has no connection to the future
challenge.explanation: The repeated pattern of watching over them connects former judgment with future restoration.
challenge.q: What does the comparison between past and future actions reveal about the Lord?

paragraphs.title: The New Covenant and Knowledge of God

answers: The house of Israel and the house of Judah
Only the nations of the sea
Only the kings of the nations
easy.explanation: The Lord says He will make a new covenant with the house of Israel and the house of Judah.
easy.q: With whom will the Lord make a new covenant?

answers: In their inward parts and hearts
easy.explanation: The Lord says, “I will put my law in their inward parts, and write it in their hearts.”
easy.q: Where will the Lord write His law?

answers: Forgive them and remember them no more
easy.explanation: The Lord promises, “I will forgive their iniquity, and I will remember their sin no more.”
easy.q: What will the Lord do concerning their sins?

answers: The law will be written inwardly in the heart
It will end the relationship with God
It will be given only to kings
medium.explanation: The new covenant emphasizes the law being placed within and written on the heart.
medium.q: How will the new covenant differ from the covenant made with the fathers?

answers: Knowing the Lord is joined with the promise of forgiveness
Knowledge comes only after punishment without mercy
medium.explanation: The passage connects universal knowledge of the Lord with forgiveness of iniquity.
medium.q: What is the relationship between knowing the Lord and forgiveness?

answers: The law will be within the people
The law will be outside the land
The law will exist only in the temple
medium.explanation: The phrase stresses an inward, personal place for God’s law.
medium.q: What does “in their inward parts” emphasize?

answers: The relationship becomes inward, known, and marked by forgiveness
challenge.explanation: The law in the heart, knowledge of God, and forgiveness describe a restored inner relationship.
challenge.q: What change in the relationship between God and Israel is emphasized?

answers: To show that knowledge of God will be universal
To say that only the important will know Him
challenge.explanation: The wording includes every member of the covenant people, regardless of status.
challenge.q: Why does the passage say that all will know the Lord, from the least to the greatest?

answers: The new covenant provides an inward relationship after the former covenant was broken
The new covenant is meant to drive Israel away
The passage never mentions the former covenant being broken
challenge.explanation: The Lord recalls that the former covenant was broken and then promises a new covenant.
challenge.q: How does the broken former covenant relate to the new covenant?

answers: The ordinances of the sun, moon, and stars
easy.explanation: The Lord compares Israel’s continued existence with the fixed ordinances of heaven.
easy.q: What illustrates Israel’s continuing existence?

easy.explanation: The Lord says, “The city shall be built to the Lord.”
easy.q: What will be rebuilt?

easy.explanation: The passage says the valley and fields “shall be holy unto the Lord.”
easy.q: What will the city and surrounding places be?

answers: They demonstrate fixed and enduring order
medium.explanation: The ordinances of the heavenly bodies illustrate stability and permanence.
medium.q: How do the sun, moon, and stars support the promise concerning Israel?

answers: The measuring describes a restored and defined city
The measuring shows that the city will be abandoned
The measuring proves the city has no boundaries
medium.explanation: The measuring line and named landmarks portray the city as rebuilt and clearly established.
medium.q: What is the connection between rebuilding the city and measuring it?

answers: The earth’s underlying bases or foundations
medium.explanation: The phrase refers to the deep foundations or bases of the earth.
medium.q: What does “the foundations of the earth” refer to?

answers: As the order of creation endures, Israel’s existence is assured
The laws of nature cancel the covenant
challenge.explanation: The Lord uses the enduring order of heaven and earth to affirm that Israel will not cease to be a nation.
challenge.q: What is the central idea in comparing the ordinances of nature with Israel?

answers: The restored area as a whole is dedicated to the Lord
The city remains unclean and deserted
challenge.explanation: The passage includes the valley, fields, brook, and gate area in the declaration of holiness.
challenge.q: What does the holiness of the city and valley signify?

answers: Return culminates in a permanent and holy city
Return has no connection with the city
challenge.explanation: The chapter moves from promises of return to the rebuilding and consecration of Jerusalem.
challenge.q: How does the ending complete the theme of return at the beginning of the chapter?
